name: Priya Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 58, an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average for the trade, doing shop lighting and household repairs rather than specialist design or running a crew. I like finding the loose connection everyone walked past, and I dislike the last-minute job that pushes supper back an hour. I use AI now and then for checked explanations after somebody has shown me a useful example, not for deciding whether an installation is safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Eli works in a hospital canteen, our children are twenty-eight and thirty-two, and we rent a ground-floor flat. My pay is typical for this work, both wages currently cover our costs, and four months of expenses are saved. There are some similar employers nearby, but I haven't applied or been offered another job. I'd like a retirement we can actually afford, although we haven't confirmed the income amount or a stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work a useful small aid can stay small. I'd keep doing repairs and only use an explanation if I could check the example for myself. I don't need every decent day with the tools to be called the start of something enormous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current pay covers the rent and ordinary costs, and four months saved makes our living feel secure. I still want to check the later retirement figures rather than guess them. Nothing radical changing would let me get on with the work without treating a quiet headline as a new problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the current licensed repair work and occasional checked AI explanations. Through the next year I'd sit with Eli each quarter over the actual wages and bills, keeping the four-month reserve for interruptions rather than spending it because the news was quieter. We'd use only confirmed income in any later stopping calculation, without assuming a pension date or either grown child's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased at the thought of doing a useful day's work without another compulsory reinvention. I'd still look at the bills on the agreed evening. A steady year would be something to enjoy, not a reason to stop paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would staying with ordinary repairs mean for responsibility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the connections and records within my licence and ordinary competence. I'm not a master electrician or the person who can promise an answer to every strange fault. Finding my own limit early is part of doing the repair properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the later calculation need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A check of the actual amounts we could receive and when, alongside the rent and other costs then. I wouldn't choose a stopping date just to make a plan look complete. A blank retirement figure is a question, not an extra wage.

say: I'd keep **small useful aids** without turning ordinary repair work into a story about a new age.
I'd use **checked examples**, keeping responsibility for the actual installation within my ordinary licence and competence.
think: Our **current wages** cover costs, and four months saved makes our household living feel secure.
I still need **real retirement figures**, without treating their absence as an immediate bill crisis.
do: Keep **current licensed repairs** and occasional checked AI explanations through the next year.
Review **actual wages and bills** quarterly with Eli, preserving the four-month reserve and using only confirmed income before any later stopping decision.
feel: **Calm and attentive**, enjoying a steady paid year while keeping the agreed household checks.

fieldNote: Her **present security** is explicit: typical pay and both wages cover costs, backed by four months saved rather than an assumed pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office that ordering and scheduling can move faster before the physical repairs do. I'd want six weeks of real paid schedules before deciding whether to learn a new scheduling aid myself. A neat demonstration isn't the same as knowing what happened to the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if quicker scheduling removed the paid gaps between jobs. Eli's canteen work looks less directly exposed to thinking tools, but our rent would still notice a cut to my wage. Four months saved gives us time to ask, not a reason to call the risk harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and occasional checked explanations while recording six weeks of actual paid hours now. I'd wait those six weeks before deciding whether to learn the new scheduling aid, reviewing earlier with Eli if either weekly wage fell. Through the first year we'd keep the quarterly actual-bill review and the reserve, with no course purchase or new AI method chosen just because the calendar had passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible shorter paid week, but willing to look at the evidence rather than reject the aid. I'd prefer a small honest table to a big argument in the van. Waiting for records doesn't mean I think the wage is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decision would you make at six weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare real paid hours and the jobs actually completed, then ask what the aid would do in my own role. If the records didn't settle the question, I wouldn't pretend six weeks had proved it useful. The review date is a chance to decide, not a booking for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one weekly wage fell before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd open the household figures sooner and use the actual lower amount, not keep waiting for the planned review. We'd check costs and what was truly available before promising any new expense. I can give a tool time to prove itself without giving a missing wage permission to hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI comes in 2028 and capable physical robots follow around 2031. I'd be 60 first and 63 later, which doesn't settle when I could afford to stop. I'd choose a short workshop with a use I could already see rather than buy an escape into another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of paid physical repair work when capable robots arrive, with planning and ordering changing earlier. That could affect Eli's canteen work too, and four months saved wouldn't settle the long household gap. I'd be awake over the unconfirmed income between wanting to stop and being able to pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd seek two paid days for a spring 2027 lighting fault-finding workshop, booking only after the employer confirmed normal weekly wages and hours would stay unchanged. I'd book only within 240 total costs, including travel, paid from wages left after essentials with Eli's agreement and the four-month reserve untouched. In 2029 I'd keep only actually offered paid repairs within my licence and ability, checking confirmed household resources with Eli before any affordable stopping decision we both agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the large later wage loss, while able to make a limited choice now. I wouldn't mistake the workshop for protection against capable robots. I want the useful practice without turning the reserve into a ticket I can't get refunded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes that particular workshop useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague took the same two-day workshop last month and showed me how the practice board exposed a lighting fault I'd met at work. That convinced me the content could help ordinary assigned jobs, not that I'd become a specialist or get hired elsewhere. A course can sharpen the electrician I am without promising a different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a booking condition could not be met?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't book if the paid-time agreement, cost ceiling or Eli's consent wasn't there. I'd keep the current repairs and use the real household figures instead of borrowing or raiding the reserve to make the workshop happen. Being worried is not a reason to sign away the conditions.

Her **conditional booking** protects paid time and cash; neither a replacement job, affordable retirement nor guaranteed work at 61 is assumed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends five years means thinking AGI in 2031, then capable robots around 2034, when I'd be 63 and 66. I'd still choose the practical workshop now, because I have lighting faults to solve before either date. I wouldn't sell the workshop as a promise of ten more paid years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid hours as planning got quicker, and I don't know what physical work or household income we'd have by the robot date. The four-month reserve is useful for an interruption, not proof of a retirement plan. There is more time to check than in the fast card, but I'd still worry about our actual wages over the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd seek the same spring 2027 workshop now, booking only after the employer confirmed two paid days with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged. All costs including travel would have to fit within 240 wages after essentials, with Eli agreeing and the four-month reserve untouched. I'd keep current licensed repairs, then in 2032 check actual resources, costs, capacity and offered work with Eli before any affordable exit we both agreed, without assuming a pension or a job at 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost paid hours, with more room to ask what is real before making the later decision. I could still value tomorrow's repair and the workshop at the same time. I don't have to call every ordinary skill either a rescue or a waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does seeing a useful example mean you will definitely enrol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I've seen the useful example, but the employer still has to confirm paid time and our household still has to meet the cost conditions. If either failed, I wouldn't book. More warning doesn't make a workshop free or turn my reserve into fees I can casually spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need at the 2032 review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual income amounts and start dates, real living costs, and whether any offered work matched my ability then. Eli and I would have to agree the affordable choice rather than put an assumed pension or a grown child's wage on the page. A later review needs the later facts, not a promise made by my present knees.

If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us longer to check choices, with thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd be 68 and then 71, so I won't write myself a guaranteed physical job for those ages. I'd still want useful practice for the jobs I actually do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages look safe over the next few years in this slower picture, and the four-month reserve still makes ordinary living manageable. What stays on my mind is how different the later work could be for younger colleagues. Our own later income and capacity need checking, but I wouldn't pretend that made next month's rent unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still seek the spring 2027 workshop for present lighting repairs, booking only after two paid days were confirmed with unchanged normal weekly wages and hours. The total including travel would stay within 240 wages after essentials, with Eli agreeing and the four-month reserve untouched. I'd keep current licensed repairs and in 2037 review actual resources, costs, capacity and real offers with Eli before an affordable jointly agreed exit, assuming neither a pension nor employment at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the wider changes, rather than frightened for our next few years' living. I can picture a younger worker needing a very different plan from ours. I'd rather be honest about that difference than borrow a worry to make myself sound thoughtful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger colleague about your workshop plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the workshop is for a fault I can meet this year, not a certificate that fixes their whole future. My plan works only within my own paid-time and household limits. An older electrician's manageable year isn't a promise to a younger colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later figures still showed a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the real gap in the figures and seek verified information before agreeing what was affordable. I wouldn't turn a grown child into an income or assume my body or an employer could supply whatever was missing. The review would have to tell us something useful, even if the answer was awkward.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the later robots to cut a large part of our physical earnings before we've confirmed an affordable way to stop. Actual paid time, a workshop cost we can meet and verified household income figures would help. I'd rather finish my working life with an honest account than with a certificate bought from the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether being willing to learn meant I wanted to keep working forever. I want useful work now and a stopping choice we can actually afford later. My licence is an electrician's licence, not a master title or a promise that someone must employ me.

headlineQuote: I'd rather finish my working life with an honest account than with a certificate bought from the rent.
portrait: Priya, **58**, is an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, doing ordinary repairs at about average skill.
Her **typical pay**, four-month reserve and canteen-worker partner Eli cover current costs; their children are grown and some similar employers are nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally**, waiting for paid-hour evidence in Steady Disruption rather than selecting new learning before the review.
Her **spring 2027 workshop** needs unchanged paid time, a 240 total-cost ceiling from surplus wages, preserved reserve and partner agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected later physical earnings losses before the household has confirmed an affordable stopping plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual paid time**, an affordable useful workshop and verified household income figures would support choices without spending the reserve or assuming retirement.
